title: Repeat until nothing changes
hints: Apply `f` once and compare the result with the input using `==`. If they're equal, you're done, and nothing changed.
If they differ, do the same again starting from the new value, and add 1 to a counter. A `while True:` loop that returns when nothing changed fits well.
Recursion is the wrong tool here: one test changes something 100,000 times, far past Python's recursion limit.
prompt:
Write fixpoint(f, x). Apply f to x, then to the result, and so on, until applying it gives back an equal value. Return that value and the number of times f changed something, as a tuple. Halving 100 with lambda n: n // 2 goes 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, 0, and then 0 // 2 is still 0, so fixpoint(lambda n: n // 2, 100) is (0, 7).

A loop and a counter. Compare with ==.

answer.explain: The loop applies `f`, returns as soon as the result equals the input, and otherwise moves to the new value and counts one change. A loop has no depth limit, so 100,000 changes are fine. That stopping rule is exactly the fixed-point loop around a rewrite pass.

tests.expr: fixpoint(lambda n: sum(int(d) for d in str(n)), 987654321)
fixpoint(lambda n: n - 10 if n > 10 else n, 95)
fixpoint(lambda l: l[1:] if len(l) > 1 and l[0] == l[1] else l, [3, 3, 3, 1])
fixpoint(lambda n: n - 1 if n > 0 else 0, 100000)
